quests.hint: Eager to succeed. Its noun, 'ambition', ends in -tion, and this adjective ends differently.
quests.explanation: Ambition becomes ambitious: the -on drops and -ous is added, leaving -tious, said /ʃəs/. The t survives from the noun.

quests.hint: Believing in luck or charms. It has five syllables and ends in -tious.
quests.explanation: Su-per-sti-tious follows the noun superstition in the same way: -tion turns into -tious. Say all five syllables before writing.

quests.hint: Intended to cause harm. Its noun, 'malice', ends in e.
quests.explanation: Malice becomes malicious: the e drops, and -ious is added. The c says /ʃ/ before -ious, as in delicious.

quests.hint: Easy to notice. Its ending is -uous, and its root means 'look'.
quests.explanation: Con-spic-u-ous has -uous, as in continuous. The root spic is a form of spec (look), also inside inspect and spectator.

quests.hint: Without a break. The verb 'continue' loses its e.
quests.explanation: Continue + ous drops the e: continuous. The ending -uous has a real u that you pronounce, giving four syllables.

quests.hint: A single person, or relating to one person. It has a u before -al.
quests.explanation: In-di-vid-u-al: five syllables ending in -ual. From Latin individuus, meaning not divisible.

quests.hint: To measure, or a measuring instrument. The vowel sound, long a, is spelled with au.
quests.explanation: Gauge has au for /eɪ/, which is unusual. The first g is hard, and the last sound /dʒ/ is written -ge.

quests.hint: A false name, especially one used by writers. It begins with a silent p.
quests.explanation: Pseu-do-nym has a silent p. Its parts are Greek: pseudes (false) and onyma (name), the same -onym as in anonymous.

quests.hint: A fatty substance found in blood. The ch says /k/, and the ending is -ol.
quests.explanation: Cho-les-ter-ol has ch for /k/, from Greek chole (bile). It ends in -ol, not -al.

quests.hint: Someone with a million pounds or dollars. It has a double l, and its ending is French.
quests.explanation: Mil-lion-aire has ll, from mille, and it ends in the French -aire, as in questionnaire. There is only one n.

quests.hint: A small fashionable shop. It ends in -tique.
quests.explanation: Bou-tique has ou for /uː/, and -tique for /tiːk/. The -que ending is the same as in unique.

quests.hint: A bunch of flowers. It ends in -quet, but you pronounce it /keɪ/.
quests.explanation: Bou-quet has ou for /uː/ and ends in -quet, said /keɪ/, with a silent t. It is a French word.

quests.hint: Loyalty to a person, country or cause. It ends in -iance.
quests.explanation: Al-le-giance has a double l, then -giance. The g is soft, and the ending -iance says /əns/.

quests.hint: The ability to recover from difficulty. Its adjective, 'resilient', ends in -ent.
quests.explanation: Resilient becomes resilience, following the -ent/-ence pairing. It ends in -ience, with i before -ence.

quests.hint: The teenage years. It has sc in the middle and ends in -ence.
quests.explanation: Ad-o-les-cence has sc for /s/ before e, from Latin adolescere (to grow up). Its adjective is adolescent.

quests.hint: To replace something older. It is the only English word that ends in -sede.
quests.explanation: Supersede is the only -sede word. Proceed, exceed and succeed end in -ceed, and the rest end in -cede.

quests.hint: To surround with armed forces, or with requests. It has ie after s.
quests.explanation: Be + siege: the prefix be- joins siege whole, and siege has the ie order (a c does not precede it). The word ends in -ege, said /iːdʒ/.

quests.hint: To grab suddenly. The long e is spelled ei, with no c before it.
quests.explanation: Seize is one of the exceptions to 'i before e', with weird, either and protein.

quests.hint: The plural of 'criterion': standards for judging. It ends in -ia.
quests.explanation: Cri-te-ri-a: a Greek plural, in which -on changes to -a. Phenomenon and phenomena work the same way.

quests.hint: Microscopic single-celled organisms. It ends in -ia, like 'criteria'.
quests.explanation: Bac-te-ri-a is the plural of bacterium, with -ium changing to -ia. It is used with a plural verb.

quests.hint: Former students of a school or university. The plural ends in -i.
quests.explanation: A-lum-ni is a Latin plural of alumnus, in which -us changes to -i. A female graduate is an alumna.

quests.hint: Impossible to manage or restrain. The stem 'control' doubles its l before -able.
quests.explanation: Un + control + l + able: the stress is on the last syllable of control, so the l doubles. The prefix adds no letter change.

quests.hint: Able to be swapped. The verb 'change' keeps its e before -able.
quests.explanation: Inter (between) + change + able keeps the e to keep the g soft, as in changeable.

quests.hint: Impossible to predict. The verb inside means 'to see in advance'.
quests.explanation: Un + foresee + able: foresee ends in a double e, and both stay before -able. The prefix fore- means 'before'.

quests.hint: Fighting against authority. The verb 'rebel' is stressed on its last syllable.
quests.explanation: Re-BEL: stress on the last syllable makes the l double before -ing. The noun REB-el is stressed at the start.

quests.hint: Performing outstandingly well. The verb 'excel' has one l, but this form has two.
quests.explanation: Ex-CEL is stressed at the end, so the l doubles before -ing: excelling. Excellent also has ll.

quests.hint: Forced to do something. The verb has its stress on the last syllable, which affects its last letter.
quests.explanation: Com-PEL is stressed on the last syllable, so the l doubles before -ed: compelled. In the noun compulsion, the stress and the spelling both change.

quests.hint: Reminding you of something. It has sc in the middle, and it ends in -ent.
quests.explanation: Rem-i-nis-cent has sc for /s/. The ending -scent, from Latin, is also in adolescent.

quests.hint: Thrilling and energising. A silent h comes after the x.
quests.explanation: Ex-hil-a-rat-ing has a silent h after ex-, as in exhausted. The verb exhilarate drops its e before -ing.

quests.hint: Extremely careful about details. It ends in -ulous.
quests.explanation: Me-tic-u-lous ends in -ulous, as ridiculous does. It has four syllables.
